# Local Apps and Browsers {#chp:apps}

R can serve web pages to itself and drive a headless browser to render them.
Together these give you a tiny local web app, plus PDFs, screenshots and
JavaScript-rendered HTML. None of the examples run here, since they start
servers or need Chrome/Chromium.

## Serve a folder in your browser {#sec:serve-dir}

To preview static files (an HTML report, a built site) over HTTP rather than
`file://`, serve the directory:

```r
serve_dir('_site')
```

In an interactive session this opens the browser. It uses R's built-in HTTP
server, so no extra packages are needed. The app is named `xfun-dir` by
default; pass `name` to serve several folders at once. Extra arguments go to
`new_app()`.

## Write your own tiny web app {#sec:new-app}

`new_app()` takes a name and a handler function `function(path, query, post,
headers)` that returns a response list. A minimal app that greets whoever is
in the query string:

```r
new_app('hello', function(path, query, post, headers) {
  who = if (is.null(query[['name']])) 'world' else query[['name']]
  list(
    payload = sprintf('<h1>Hello, %s!</h1>', who),
    `content-type` = 'text/html'
  )
}, open = FALSE)
```

It returns the URL invisibly, something like `http://127.0.0.1:PORT/custom/hello/`.
Visit it with `?name=R` to see the query used. With `name = ''` the app is
served at the root `http://127.0.0.1:PORT/` through a small proxy, and `port`
picks the candidate ports. Calling `new_app()` with an existing name replaces
that app.

In a non-interactive script, `open` also decides whether the call blocks.
Pass `open = FALSE` explicitly to return right away.

## Shut an app down {#sec:stop-app}

Apps live as long as the R session. Stop one by name, or all of them:

```r
stop_app('hello')
stop_app()  # every running app
```

## Print a page to PDF or an image {#sec:browser-print}

`browser_print()` loads a page in headless Chrome, Chromium, or Edge and
saves it. The output extension picks the format: `.pdf`, `.png`, or `.jpeg`.
A bare extension reuses the name from the input:

```r
browser_print('report.html')                    # report.pdf
browser_print('report.html', 'shot.png')        # screenshot
browser_print('https://www.r-project.org', '.jpeg', window_size = c(800, 600))
```

It returns the output path. If the browser is not found, set
`options(xfun.browser = '/path/to/chrome')` or the `R_XFUN_BROWSER`
environment variable.

For pages that finish rendering after load, use `wait` with a JavaScript
expression that becomes true when the page is ready, or a named event. `query`
appends URL parameters:

```r
browser_print('slides.html', wait = 'window.pageReady', query = list(print = 1))
browser_print('slides.html', wait = c(event = 'pageReady'))
```

## See the HTML after JavaScript runs {#sec:browser-dom}

The source of a page that builds itself with JavaScript is nearly empty.
`browser_dom()` loads it, lets the scripts run, and gives back the final DOM:

```r
f = tempfile(fileext = '.html')
writeLines(c(
  '<html><body><div id="out"></div>',
  '<script>document.getElementById("out").textContent = "hello";</script>',
  '</body></html>'
), f)
browser_dom(f)                  # full document as a string
browser_dom(f, fragment = TRUE) # only the inner body
browser_dom(f, output = 'rendered.html')
```

It takes `wait` and `query` like `browser_print()`.

## Run many JavaScript checks in one browser {#sec:browser-session}

Starting a browser per page is slow. `browser_session()` starts one and keeps
it open. You get a list of functions: `open()` to load a page, `eval()` to run
JavaScript on it, `dom()` for the current HTML, and `close()`:

```r
s = browser_session()
for (p in c('a.html', 'b.html')) {
  s$open(p)
  print(s$eval('document.title'))
}
s$dom()
s$close()
```

`eval()` returns the value of the last statement as a string. The browser also
closes when the session is garbage-collected or R exits, but calling `close()`
is tidier.
